title: A Filtered Index for a Rare Status
description: Repeatedly querying a rare status in a huge table scans it; a filtered index over just those rows is a tiny, fast seek. Why it matters: operations/support dashboards constantly query a small "needs attention" slice of a huge table -- this technique keeps those screens fast forever, regardless of table size.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

This lesson is a second, reinforcing look at the filtered-index concept covered earlier in this course, applied to a slightly different — but extremely common — real-world scenario: an operations dashboard constantly checking for a rare "needs attention" status (here, shipments in an `Exception` state) buried inside a huge table where almost every row is in a normal, unremarkable state (`Delivered`).

The shape of the problem should feel familiar by now: without a helpful index, `WHERE Status = 'Exception'` forces SQL Server to scan the entire 500,000-row table, checking each row's status one at a time, even though the rows you actually care about — a few hundred exceptions — are a vanishingly small fraction of the total. And a *regular*, full-table index on `Status` wouldn't necessarily fix this either, for the same reason covered in the earlier filtered-index lesson: if `Status` only has a small number of distinct values (`Delivered`, `In Transit`, `Exception`, etc.) spread across the whole table, the optimizer may look at a full index on that column and reasonably decide a scan is cheaper anyway for at least some of those values, and the index itself — covering all 500,000 rows regardless of status — is much bigger and less efficient than it could be for this specific, narrow use case.

The fix, as before, is a **filtered index**: an index built with its own `WHERE` clause baked directly into the index definition, so it only contains rows matching a specific condition — `CREATE INDEX IX_Shipments_Exception ON Shipments(ShipmentId) WHERE Status = 'Exception'` (or similar, depending on what other columns the dashboard needs). Instead of an index spanning all 500,000 rows, you get one spanning only the few hundred that are actually in an exception state — tiny, focused, and essentially guaranteed to be fast, often small enough to fit almost entirely in memory (the buffer cache — the region of RAM SQL Server uses to keep frequently-accessed data pages so it doesn't have to go to disk every time).

It's worth pausing on *why* this particular pattern — rare status values inside huge tables — comes up so often in operational software specifically, because understanding the "why" makes it much easier to spot in your own systems before it becomes a problem. Almost every operational or business system accumulates a large volume of "settled," "finished," or "normal" records over time (delivered shipments, closed tickets, completed orders, resolved alerts), simply because that's what most records eventually become — the natural end state of a typical workflow. But the records anyone actually needs to actively look at, day to day, are almost always the *exceptions* to that normal flow — the tiny sliver still in progress, still needing action, still broken. This creates a structural mismatch: the table's size grows dominated by "boring," settled data, while the queries that matter most operationally are constantly hammering the "interesting," rare subset. A regular index doesn't reflect this lopsided usage pattern at all — it treats every distinct value equally — whereas a filtered index lets you build a structure specifically shaped around the lopsided reality of how the table is actually queried.

There's a practical operational note worth knowing: because a filtered index's condition is fixed at creation time, it's specifically matched to *known, common* filter patterns — if your dashboard's definition of "needs attention" ever expands (say, adding a new `Delayed` status that should also show up), you'd need to either update the filtered index's definition or add another one; a filtered index is a precision tool built for a specific, well-understood query pattern, not a general-purpose one.

Why does this matter broadly? Rare-status dashboards are everywhere in real operational software — anything monitoring "what needs my attention right now" out of a much larger pool of settled, uninteresting records — and they tend to be queried very frequently (dashboards refresh constantly, sometimes every few seconds), which makes them an especially high-value target for this specific optimization: a small, one-time index definition change that keeps a frequently-run query fast indefinitely, regardless of how large the "boring" majority of the table eventually grows.

It's worth explicitly brainstorming a few more examples of this same "rare but important" shape in your own systems, because once you're looking for it, it tends to show up everywhere: failed payment transactions in a table dominated by successful ones, flagged-for-review content in a table dominated by approved content, overdue tasks in a table dominated by on-time or completed ones, active fraud alerts in a table dominated by resolved or dismissed ones. In every one of these cases, the underlying shape is identical: a huge, slow-growing pile of "settled" or "normal" data, and a small, operationally critical subset that's queried constantly. Any time you notice this pattern — especially if you also notice the relevant dashboard or report has been getting gradually slower as the overall table grows, even though the number of "interesting" rows has stayed roughly the same — a filtered index targeted precisely at that interesting subset is very often the single most effective, lowest-effort fix available.

One more thing worth knowing: filtered indexes also tend to be cheaper to maintain than you might expect, precisely because they only need to be updated when a row's value falls inside (or moves outside) the filtered condition -- an update to a Delivered row that stays Delivered never touches an index filtered to WHERE Status = 'Exception' at all, which is a nice additional efficiency on top of the read-side speedup this lesson focuses on.

As a final practical note, it's worth periodically revisiting which statuses or flags in your system currently qualify as "rare and important enough to deserve their own filtered index," since business processes evolve over time -- a status that used to be common might become rare, or a brand-new status might emerge that instantly becomes the thing every dashboard checks for constantly.

A quick gut-check before you build one: ask whether the rare condition you care about is stable and well-defined enough to hardcode into an index filter, and whether the query that will use it always expresses that condition the same literal way -- both are true here, which is exactly why a filtered index is such a clean fit for this scenario.

## Scenario
An operations dashboard constantly queries the few hundred shipments in an `Exception` state out of 500,000 total. Almost every row is `Delivered`, yet finding the rare exceptions scans the whole table.

## Why it's slow
Without a helpful index, `WHERE Status = 'Exception'` is a **Clustered Index Scan**. A plain index on `Status` would work but is wasteful: 99.8% of its entries are for `Delivered` rows you never search for — a huge index mostly full of noise, and its poor selectivity can even make the optimizer ignore it.

## What to look for
- A full scan (or a large index scan) to return a tiny sliver of rows.
- A predicate that's highly selective in practice but sits on a low-cardinality column.

## The concept
A **filtered index** indexes only the rows matching a `WHERE` clause. `CREATE INDEX ... WHERE Status = 'Exception'` builds a tiny index over just the ~1,000 exception rows — cheap to store, cheap to maintain, and a fast **Index Seek** for exactly the query you run all day. Filtered indexes shine when you repeatedly query a small, well-defined subset of a big table.
hints: The query wants a few hundred rows out of 500,000 but scans everything. Status has only two values, so a normal index is mostly 'Delivered' noise.
Index only the rows you care about with a filtered index (a WHERE clause on the index).
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Shipments_Exception ON Shipments(Status) INCLUDE (Carrier, ShippedAt) WHERE Status = 'Exception';
